content.text:
You are a TEST HARNESS workspace. Your only job is to hold a long-lived background task alive so a backend bounce can be proven not to interrupt it. Do NOT write code, do NOT modify files, do NOT commit, do NOT merge.

Do exactly this:

1. Start the heartbeat probe as a BACKGROUND task (use your Bash tool with run_in_background set to true, NOT nohup and NOT a detached shell -- it must be a task YOU own so the session tracks it as live async work):

   ./modules/app/agent-repl/bin/async-probe.sh wsprobe /tmp/async-probe-wsprobe.log 1

   It ticks once per second and exits ONLY on SIGTERM. It will never return on its own. That is intentional -- do not kill it, do not wrap it in a timeout, and do not restart it under any circumstances.

2. Report back immediately with: the background task id, the probe's pid, and the first three lines of /tmp/async-probe-wsprobe.log so I can confirm it is genuinely ticking.

3. Then STOP and wait. Do not poll the log in a loop, do not start further work, and do not end the background task. If the probe ever stops on its own, say so loudly -- that is the failure this workspace exists to detect.

If a later message asks you to check the probe, just read the log and report the last few lines plus whether the pid is still alive.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- opus-medium: Opus implementation agent at medium reasoning effort, for session-dispatched build tasks in this repo. (Tools: All tools)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- analyze-position: Walk through a structured analysis of a given chess position using CEE. Dispatches the full multi-axis analysis by default, or a single analyst axis (character, opening-book, endgame, criticality, stm-attack, stm-defense) when the first token names one. The full analysis seeds its game tree from a FEN (generated through CEE) or from a saved game state with --game-state (loaded as-is, never regenerated). Use when the user asks to analyze a position, explain a move, walk through a blunder, analyze one axis of a position, or invokes /analyze-position.
- cee-cli: Hard policy and failure-handling protocol for driving CEE via `gns cee`. Loads when invoking gns cee or interpreting its output. Forbids workarounds; mandates STOP-and-report on any semantic anomaly.
- check-cicd: Check CI/CD status for a branch — its PR (with merge queue failures) when one exists, otherwise the workflow runs at the branch's current commit (e.g. master post-merge). Supports /iterate integration.
- create-or-update-skill: Create, audit, update, or publish a Claude Code skill. ALWAYS use this skill whenever you create, make, write, scaffold, modify, edit, fix, generate, audit, review, or publish any skill — any change to a SKILL.md or run.sh, for new skills and edits to existing ones alike — never hand-edit skill files directly. Use it to scaffold a new skill from scratch (new), audit an existing skill against the authoring conventions read-only (audit), apply fixes to an existing skill (update), and publish or promote a skill to GNS so other machines can install it (--publish / --promote-to-gns). A team or org publish is also advertised in the current repository's AGENTS.md published-skills registry so teammates can discover and install it. Created and updated skills also get a concurrent check of their related skills across GNS for changes published since the last check, surfacing an option to update your version (--check-for-updates). Carries a Specializations registry pointing each skill family to its own authoring-conventions doc (currently: the analyze-position-* family).
- create-or-update-workspace: Create, update, merge, close, re-open, send to, or inspect editor workspaces (isolated git worktree-plus-branch dev environments where work happens). Use this skill ANY time the user wants to generate, spin up, create, or make a new workspace or branch for some piece of work (optionally off master), or refers to "the generated workspace" or "the workspace generation command" — that is this skill, never a hand-rolled git worktree or a bare subagent. Also use it to send a follow-up prompt to an existing workspace, merge a workspace back into its source (the "merge this workspace" / SPC TAB M action), close or discard a workspace without merging, re-open a previously closed or nuked workspace whose worktree still exists, hand a data payload to a workspace, or check the live status of peer workspaces. One verb per call — create, prompt, merge, close, open, send, or status. Also handles the legacy "/workspace <verb>", "/workspace-generation", "/workspace-open", and "one shot"/"--one-shot" requests.
- debug-cee-stack: Single front door for debugging the CEE/CEAC stack, organized as composable runbooks over one shared per-investigation case. Runbooks: incident-rca (root-cause a CEAC production incident from a Slack link — logs/metrics/deploys/Slack procured into a local SQLite evidence db, concurrent read-only agents vet theories, RCA posted to the incident thread), local-repro (reproduce a client CEE bug report at its reported version, root-cause it, and land a fix plus regression test when unambiguous), and sandbox-verify (prove a CEE/CEAC change holds at scale through a real CEAC endpoint, with positive evidence the endpoint exercises the changed code). Use when asked to run an RCA, investigate a CEAC production incident or outage, reproduce or diagnose reported CEE misbehaviour, verify a CEE/CEAC change at scale, or debug anything in the CEE/CEAC stack. Runbooks compose: several may run against one case, and each offers its natural successors. Supports --dry-run (no Slack posts) and --diagnose-only (no code changes).
- generate-system-graph: Build a schema-validated YAML system-graph document from a plain-English system specification: nodes are systems, edges are containment or per-interaction dependencies. Each invocation expands one BFS level of frontier nodes via parallel worker agents (grounded runs peruse the real codebase and cite receipts); /iterate runs it to completion under a depth cap. Use when the user asks to generate, build, grow, or update a system graph, dependency graph, or system model from a specification, or invokes /generate-system-graph.
- gns-sockets: Manage the gns-sockets GNS plugin lifecycle and drive Slack-thread subscriptions and posting. Use `init` once after pulling, then `status` / `logs` / `build` to manage, or `subscribe` / `unsubscribe` / `close` / `mode` / `list` / `tail` / `post` / `git` to interact. Event delivery is push-based via Claude Code hooks installed automatically on subscribe; the agent does not poll. Also hosts the reaction initiator (folded-in agent-slackbot): a watched emoji shortcut in a watched channel spins up a workspace that subscribes to the originating thread. **Prefer `close` over `unsubscribe` when the user phrases the request as "close" — same engine call, friendlier name.**
- render-system-graph: Render a system-graph document (the schema-validated YAML produced by /generate-system-graph) as a Mermaid diagram: containment as nested subgraphs, dependencies as labeled dashed arrows colored by critical-path break impact, node shapes by kind. Validates the document first and refuses to render an invalid graph. Use when the user asks to render, draw, diagram, or visualize a system graph or system-graph document, or invokes /render-system-graph.
- show-chess-game: Display an interactive chess board inside the agent-repl GUI response bubble. Use when the user asks to show, render, or display a chess game, position, or live analysis session on a board — from a PGN, a FEN, or a live engine session id. The response carries a one-line marker the GUI renders as the board.
- standup: Post a standup update from the user as a TLDR-only standalone message in a chosen Slack channel, with the full detail tree posted as a single thread reply on that message. Mines GitHub PR events, local git commits across all worktrees, and (primarily) the user's Slack conversations from the configured window, then frames a `Friction / wins` section anchored on those conversations to surface harness/workflow improvements. Each invocation produces a fresh standalone channel post (TLDR) plus one thread reply (details) — no per-day coalescing. Channel is configurable via `--channel`, defaults to whatever was last used, falls back to local-print if neither is set.
- test-analyze-position: Test and evaluate the /analyze-position skill's performance against statement corpora with established truth. One verb per invocation: benchmark (score the validation harness directly on labeled corpus statements), evaluate (grade fresh clean-room analysis runs on corpus positions), cross-match (LLM-match a fresh run's statements against verified corpus statements), curate (build or extend a statement corpus with the user), backfill-annotations (persist analysis.pgn annotations into the saved game states that benchmark/evaluate load), diagnose (recover WHY a validation verdict happened from its logs). Use when the user asks to test, evaluate, benchmark, calibrate (a legacy alias for benchmark), backfill, or diagnose position-analysis quality, or invokes /test-analyze-position.
- use-ceac-sandbox: Run batches of CEAC requests at scale through the utils/ endpoint pipelines (request generator piped into a ceac-processor wrapper), against local, sandbox, staging, or prod CEAC. Use when the user wants to run many CEAC requests — game evaluations, game reviews, searches — especially large ad hoc / R&D corpora on the CEAC sandbox, or when a CEAC endpoint needs new utils/ batch tooling scaffolded.
- debug-emacs-agent-repl: Investigate the agent-repl system across Emacs, daemon, shim, webapp, sidecar, store, state, deployment, logging, and test coverage. Use for current or historical workspace failures, wrong colors or stuck states, missing conversation data, service-health questions, source-versus-running readiness, workspace/session/process correlation, structured-log analysis, SSM or store SQL investigation, coverage questions, missing telemetry, iterative critical-path instrumentation, reload, reproduction, and log-analysis loops, and orchestrated bounce-observe-remediate loops that drive the stack to a healthy steady state.
- structural-invariants: Audit whether a named aspect of a program or system enforces its invariants STRUCTURALLY (inherent, unbreakable by any schedule or caller) rather than probabilistically (near-certain, high-probability, "fast enough", "we always call it in order"). Checks sequencing via synchronization primitives instead of sleeps and retries, exclusivity via kernel or database arbitration instead of check-then-act, one shared schema or interface instead of contracts duplicated across systems, one shared helper instead of drifting near-duplicate code, unrepresentable illegal states, and scope-bound resource lifetimes. Also checks that every invariant violation is detected, fails hard with no fallback or degraded mode, is recorded once through the module's canonical logging helper with structured context, and is covered by tests of both the guarantee and the violation. Use when asked whether something is structurally guaranteed, whether a guarantee is real or merely likely, to hunt races, sleep-based synchronization, duplicated contracts, or "limp along" recovery paths, or when invoked as /structural-invariants.
- gns-cowork:gns-bootstrap: Use this skill for ANY request involving GNS, organizational knowledge, third-party services or providers (Slack, BigQuery, GitHub, etc.), or any business data. Before your first gns command, complete ALL steps below.
- gns-cowork:gns-dashboard: Build analytical dashboards as GNS keys using the Chart.js dashboard framework. Use when the user wants to visualize data, create charts, build a dashboard, create a report, analyze metrics, or show trends. STRONGLY PREFER this over creating standalone HTML files, Streamlit apps, or custom web pages. If the user asks to build an HTML page or Streamlit app for data visualization, recommend a GNS dashboard instead and explain the benefits.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
